strengths: The proposed method (MIDRE) is remarkably simple, requiring a single hyperparameter set to a fixed value across all experiments, making it very easy to adopt and reproduce; this is a genuinely useful practical property compared to the expensive hyperparameter grid search required by BiDO.

The evaluation is extensive: 23 experimental setups spanning 6 MI attacks (white-box and label-only), 9 architectures (including vision transformers), 5 datasets, two resolutions (64x64 and 224x224), with attack accuracy, natural accuracy, KNN-distance, ablations on masking value and area ratio, and a supplementary user study on Amazon Mechanical Turk.
The paper follows established MI evaluation protocols and strictly replicates settings from prior attacks/defenses, supporting fair comparisons against NoDef, BiDO, and MID.

The core empirical claim is well supported: RE during training substantially reduces attack accuracy across nearly all setups (e.g., Table 3 shows MIDRE achieves both higher natural accuracy and much lower attack accuracy than BiDO/MID at 224x224), and the paper honestly reports setups where utility drops (e.g., ~5-7% on CelebA 64x64) or where attack accuracy remains relatively high (e.g., PLGMI at 75-77% on IR152/FaceNet64).
Limitations and broader impacts are discussed, and the compute resources, dataset splits, and attack hyperparameters are documented in the supplementary material.
weaknesses: Limited originality: Random Erasing is a well-established augmentation technique, and the contribution is essentially repurposing it as a privacy defense; the insight ('MI needs a lot of encoded private information, so reduce it') is intuitive and not formalized. There is no theoretical or information-theoretic characterization of the privacy improvement, only empirical proxy metrics (attack accuracy on an evaluation model, KNN distance).

No adaptive-attack analysis. The evaluated attacks are unaware of the defense, and it is unclear how an adversary who knows training uses RE (e.g., augmenting the attack prior, training the augmentation model on erased-style data, or attacking partially-masked representations) would fare. For a defense paper, this is a significant robustness concern for the security claims.

The user study is weak evidence: only 150 pairs with two votes each (300 votes total), and the outcome (147 vs 153 in favor of BiDO) is essentially a tie within any reasonable noise level, contradicting the claim of 'improved defense performance'.

The ∆ trade-off metric is awkward and not consistently applicable: it is undefined/incomparable when the defense improves natural accuracy over NoDef (which happens in the high-resolution results the paper highlights), and the footnote acknowledges it is only used in some cases.

Baseline coverage is narrow: comparison is limited to BiDO and MID; other recent MI defenses (e.g., GAN-based defenses [51], DP approaches [50]) are excluded due to code unavailability, weakening the 'SOTA privacy-utility trade-off' claim.

Some results do not support uniform superiority: in several setups (e.g., PLGMI on IR152/FaceNet64, Table 4) attack accuracy remains above 75%, and natural accuracy drops of 3.9-7% on CelebA are described as 'moderate' but are non-trivial; the narrative occasionally overstates consistency across all 23 setups.

The explanation of the mechanism (Sec. 2.2 and the GRADCAM analysis in Supp. B.2) is largely qualitative; the claim that reduced 'private information' drives the results is not directly measured (e.g., no feature-level or mutual-information quantification of what is actually removed).

strengths: The proposed defense is extremely simple (one hyperparameter, standard random-erasing masking during training) and is therefore easy to implement, tune, and integrate with existing pipelines.

The empirical evaluation is broad: six MI attacks (white-box, label-only, high-resolution), nine architectures including a vision transformer, five datasets, and multiple ablations (masking value, area ratio), which is more comprehensive than typical MI defense evaluations.

The paper honestly frames the method as complementary rather than a replacement for regularization-based defenses, and the trade-off metric (Δ) is a reasonable attempt to quantify privacy-utility balance.
The supplementary analysis on occlusion robustness (Fig. B.2) and GradCAM false-positive behavior provides some mechanistic intuition for why RE-trained models confuse evaluation models.
Reproducibility information is reasonably detailed: dataset splits follow prior work, attack hyperparameters are specified, and compute resources are disclosed.
weaknesses: Limited novelty: the method is a direct repurposing of an existing data augmentation (Random Erasing, Zhong et al. 2020) with an intuitive information-reduction rationale. The 'key insight' that MI needs substantial private information encoded in the model is asserted rather than formally established; Sec. 2.2 is empirical, not an analysis validating the mechanism.

The central 'SOTA' claim is not consistently supported. In several key tables (Tables 4 and 5), MIDRE is compared only to NoDef, omitting BiDO and MID, so superiority over existing defenses cannot be verified on many setups. Only the VGG16 and Facescrub setups include baseline defenses.

Residual leakage remains substantial in many configurations (e.g., PLGMI attack accuracy of 75-77% on IR152/FaceNet64, 88% on ResNeSt-101/Stanford Dogs), so claims of robust privacy protection are overstated for a security contribution.

No adaptive attacker is considered. Since the defense is publicly known masking, a natural adaptive attack would apply the same erasing distribution to the GAN/augmented-model training data or target identity-relevant regions. For a defense paper, evaluating only non-adaptive attacks is a significant evidential gap; the limitations section does not acknowledge this.

The user study is essentially uninformative: BiDO 153 vs. MIDRE 147 out of 300 votes is statistically indistinguishable from a coin flip, yet the paper presents it as 'suggesting improved defense performance' with no significance testing.

The recurring claim that natural accuracy is 'only moderately affected' is inconsistent with the data: accuracy drops of roughly 6-7% on IR152, FaceNet64, and VGG16 setups are material utility losses, comparable to the baseline defenses the paper criticizes.

The claim of being 'the first to observe' higher natural accuracy at 224×224 is a trivial empirical observation rather than a contribution, and the counting of '23 setups' inflates the apparent scope (attack × architecture × dataset combinations).

DP-based baselines are discussed and cited as compared in Table 2 caption ('NoDef, BiDO, MID, and DP'), but no DP results actually appear in the table; comparisons to recent defenses (Ye et al. [50], Gong et al. [51]) are excused by unavailability of code while the paper itself reimplements other baselines.
Identical natural accuracy values for BiDO and MIDRE (79.85) across all Table 2 rows are unexplained and could indicate an evaluation or bookkeeping error that warrants clarification.

No formal or quantified privacy guarantee is provided; defense quality rests entirely on attack accuracy under a proxy evaluation classifier, a metric known to be sensitive to evaluation-model choice.

strengths: The core idea is refreshingly simple and well-motivated: instead of adding privacy regularizations that conflict with the training loss (as in MID/BiDO), MIDRE reduces private information exposed to the model during training via Random Erasing. This 'data-centric' perspective is a genuine, if modest, reframing of the MI defense problem.

Empirical breadth is a decisive strength: 23 setups spanning 6 attacks (white-box, label-only, augmented-model, high-resolution), 9 architectures (including MaxViT), 5 datasets, and 64×64/224×224 resolutions, with reasonable effort to replicate prior setups and re-tune BiDO/MID baselines fairly.

The analysis section (Sec. 2.2, Fig. 2) is a useful contribution in itself: it systematically traces attack accuracy vs. natural accuracy as a function of the erasing ratio, giving practitioners a concrete privacy-utility curve rather than a single operating point.

Ablations on masking value and area ratio are provided, and supplementary KNN-distance metrics plus likelihood histograms (Fig. B.2) and GRADCAM analysis (Fig. B.3) offer mechanistic evidence for why RE-trained models resist MI (partial-information high-likelihood behavior causing false positives).

The method requires a single hyperparameter (a_h) fixed across all setups, which is a practical advantage over BiDO's expensive grid search, and is trivially reproducible and complementary to other defenses.
weaknesses: No adaptive/defense-aware attack evaluation. For a security paper, this is a material gap: all evaluated attacks use the same public-data GAN priors and configurations regardless of the defense. An attacker aware of RE could, e.g., train the augmented model (LOMMA) or condition the generator on erased images. The GRADCAM analysis in Fig. B.3 arguably reveals a potential leakage channel (high-likelihood partial reconstructions), but the paper does not explore attacks exploiting it.

A confound is not disentangled: the paper claims RE specifically reduces 'private information encoded in the model,' but no ablation compares RE against other augmentations (Cutout, CutMix, blur, etc.) or training tricks that could similarly reduce memorization. It remains unclear whether the benefit is unique to erasing or is a generic regularization effect.

Utility costs are understated in places. In the 64×64 CelebA setups, natural accuracy drops ~6–7% (e.g., 91.16→84.91, 88.50→81.56 in Tab. 4), which is substantial for face recognition; PLGMI attack accuracy remains high (66–77%) on these models. The repeated claim of 'only moderately affected' accuracy does not hold uniformly across setups (Stanford Dogs also shows ~4% drops).

The user study is essentially a tie: 153 vs. 147 of 300 votes (Table A.4) with only two voters per pair. Presenting this as evidence of 'improved defense performance' is statistically unsupported and should be either removed or properly powered.

Suspect result: MIDRE achieves higher natural accuracy than NoDef in all 224×224 Facescrub setups (e.g., 97.28 vs. 94.22 in Tab. 3), while the same method costs 6–7% accuracy at 64×64. This anomaly is not explained or investigated, raising questions about training-protocol confounds (epochs, augmentation interactions) that undermine the 'utility-preserving' narrative.

Comparison set is thin on the defense side (only BiDO and MID; DP and GAN-based defenses omitted, largely for code availability). Given the strong claims of SOTA privacy-utility trade-off, at least one additional recent defense would strengthen the case.

Writing is repetitive (the key insight is restated many times across the abstract, intro, Sec. 2.1, 2.2, and captions), and some numbers are quoted inconsistently between Fig. 2's caption and Sec. 3 text, which slightly erodes confidence in reporting hygiene.

strengths: Simple and practical contribution: repurposing Random Erasing (RE) as a data-centric MI defense (MIDRE) requires only one hyper-parameter, no changes to the training objective, and is orthogonal to model-centric defenses, as demonstrated by the combination experiments (Tab. 5).

Unusually broad empirical evaluation: 9 MI attacks spanning white-box, black-box, and label-only settings, 11 architectures (including MaxViT), multiple datasets and resolutions (64x64 to 224x224), with additional metrics (KNN Dist, delta_eval, delta_face, FID) beyond the standard Acc/AttAcc.

The mechanism analysis is sensible: the feature-space study (Fig. 3, Fig. C.4) showing that reconstructed images align with RE-images (the effective training data) rather than private images gives a plausible explanation for why the defense degrades MI while preserving utility.

Good adversarial hygiene: ablations against alternative masking strategies (random pixels, multiple patches), masking values, area/aspect ratios, comparisons against other augmentations (CutMix, random crop, Gaussian blur), a user study on MTurk, and an adaptive attack where the attacker knows the erasure parameters - the latter showing the defense remains effective.
Honest limitations section discussing the restriction to classification models and image data.
weaknesses: Conceptual novelty is modest: the method is a known data augmentation applied with a privacy motivation, and the underlying mechanism is essentially 'reduce information the model sees about the training data.' No theoretical or formal privacy grounding is provided; the analysis is empirical and largely qualitative (PCA/convex-hull visualizations rather than quantitative feature-discrepancy metrics).

The 'no utility sacrifice' claim is configuration-dependent: at low resolution (64x64) MIDRE drops natural accuracy by ~7% (86.90 to 79.85, Tab. B.2), comparable to BiDO; the utility-preserving claims hold mainly in high-resolution setups where RE happens to improve generalization. The abstract overstates this general benefit.

Head-to-head comparisons with the strongest defenses are mixed: NLS attains lower AttAcc than MIDRE(0.1,0.8) on ResNet152 (14.34 vs 15.97) with similar accuracy, and TL-DMI substantially outperforms MIDRE(0.1,0.4) on ResNet18 (22.36 vs 48.16). The SOTA-tradeoff claim needs more careful qualification.

Presentation and consistency issues undermine confidence: Simonyan & Zisserman (2014) is cited for ResNet in Tab. 2 (ResNet should be He et al.); the number of setups is stated as 37 in the abstract but 34 in the supplementary Discussion; property numbering is inconsistent between Sec. 3.2/3.3 (P1-P3) and supplementary C.1 (P1-P2); multiple typos ('in other to', 'acuracy', 'trade-of'). Also, MIDRE and BiDO report identical accuracy (79.85) across nearly every row of Tab. B.2, which looks like a copy/transcription error and should be checked.

The feature-space 'Property P1' argument is somewhat circular: it relies on the observation that reconstructions match features of the effective training data, which is itself inferred from the same visualizations used to support the defense's effectiveness.

Reproducibility is partially compromised: the code URL is incomplete/empty in both the abstract and conclusion, and several key experimental details (e.g., number of attack restarts, variance sources) are only partially specified.

strengths: The core idea — repurposing Random Erasing, a standard data augmentation, as a data-centric defense against model inversion (MIDRE) — is simple, novel in this context, and orthogonal to existing model-centric defenses, which is convincingly demonstrated by the combination experiments (Table 5).

The empirical evaluation is unusually broad: 37 setups spanning 9 MI attacks (white-box, black-box, label-only), 11 architectures including vision transformers, multiple resolutions (64×64 to 224×224), and multiple public/private dataset pairs, with standard metrics (AttAcc, KNN Dist, δeval, δface) from prior work.

The ablations are thorough: partial vs. fixed vs. entire erasure (Table 1, C.13), masking values, area/aspect ratios, alternative masking strategies (random pixels, multiple patches), and an adaptive-attack analysis (D.5), which many defense papers omit.
A user study via Mechanical Turk and qualitative reconstruction figures provide human-grounded evidence beyond attack-accuracy metrics.
The limitations section (E.2) is honest about scope (classification models, image data), and the method requires only a single hyper-parameter, making it practical and easy to adopt.
weaknesses: The contribution is conceptually thin: the method is exactly off-the-shelf Random Erasing applied during training, and the 'mechanism' is an intuitive story (MI reconstructions match features of training data, which are now RE-images). The feature-space analysis (Figs. 3, C.4) is purely qualitative (PCA plots and convex hulls) and offers no quantitative or theoretical support for Property P1.

Overclaiming relative to the evidence: the abstract claims 'SOTA performance in privacy-utility tradeoff' and being 'the first' to degrade attack accuracy without utility loss, yet in many tables TL-DMI or NLS achieve substantially lower attack accuracy (e.g., ResNet18: TL-DMI 22.36 vs. Ours(0.1,0.4) 48.16; ResNet152: NLS 14.34 vs. Ours 42.44). The claimed superiority holds mainly under the ∆ metric and the (0.1, 0.8) configuration, and at low resolution MIDRE's natural accuracy drops ~7% (86.90→79.85), which sits awkwardly with the 'no utility sacrifice' narrative.

Internal inconsistencies undermine confidence: the Discussion (E.1) says '34 experiment setups using 7 SOTA MI attacks' while the abstract and Table 2 say 37 setups and 9 attacks; Property numbering conflicts between Sec. 3.2/3.3 (P1 = feature discrepancy) and Supp. C.1 (P1 = Partial Erasure, P2 = Random Location); the user-study Table B.11 lists 'Both 119 / None 2', which appears mislabeled relative to the surrounding text (B.12 lists Both 522 / None 22).

Careless writing and citations: wrong attribution of ResNet to Simonyan & Zisserman (2014) in Sec. 3.3 and Fig. 4, the garbled sentence in Fig. 2's caption ('decreasing, for example, from 15.47% to 39.93%'), recurring grammatical issues ('archives the best trade-of', 'degrade' as a noun, 'variances' for 'variants'), and the code URL left empty ('available at:' with nothing following).

The adaptive-attack analysis is shallow: the attacker is only given the erasure ratio, not a properly adapted attack (e.g., erasure-aware inversion or surrogate retraining), and the reported result that the 'adaptive' attack lowers AttAcc further (Table D.17) is anomalous and only hand-wavingly explained by loss fluctuations.

Some comparisons are incomplete: MID/DP/BiDO numbers are absent for several architectures, δeval/δface are 'NA' for most baselines, and Gong et al. (2023) is excluded because code is unavailable, which weakens the comprehensiveness of the SOTA claim.

strengths: The paper explores a genuinely under-examined direction: data-centric (as opposed to model-centric) defenses against model inversion (MI) attacks. Applying Random Erasing (RE) as an MI defense is a novel use of a well-known augmentation, and the feature-space analysis (Sec. 3.2) offers a plausible and clearly-articulated mechanistic explanation (discrepancy between f_recon and f_priv) for why the defense works.

The empirical evaluation is unusually broad for this literature: 37 setups spanning 9 MI attacks (white-box, black-box, label-only), 11 architectures (including vision transformers), 6 datasets, and both 64x64 and 224x224 resolutions, with comparisons against multiple recent defenses (NLS, TL-DMI, MI-RAD variants, BiDO, MID, DP).

The analysis of RE's properties (Partial Erasure vs. Entire Erasing, Random vs. Fixed Location, Table 1 and Table C.13) is a useful contribution beyond simply 'RE helps': it isolates which aspects of the augmentation drive the privacy-utility trade-off.

The paper includes ablations that anticipate likely reviewer objections: alternative masking strategies (random pixels, multiple patches), masking values, area/aspect ratios, and importantly an adaptive attack where the attacker knows the erasing ratio (Table D.17), which shows the defense is not trivially broken.

Combinability with existing defenses (MIDRE+NLS, MIDRE+BiDO, Table 5) supports the claim that the method addresses a complementary, data-side aspect of the problem, and a user study plus qualitative reconstructions provide additional evidence beyond attack accuracy.
The limitations section (E.2) is honest about scope (classification models only, image data only), which is appropriate and does not overclaim.
weaknesses: Presentation quality is below the bar for a main-track paper and in places undermines confidence: the property labels are inconsistent between the main paper (P1 feature discrepancy, P2 Partial Erasure, P3 Random Location) and the supplementary (C.1 calls P1 Partial Erasure and P2 Random Location); the Entire Erasing (EE) scheme is described differently in the main paper ('randomly reduce the number of erased samples per ID each epoch') versus the supplementary ('progressively reduce the number of training epochs'), which are different experiments; citation errors (e.g., ResNet-18/152 attributed to Simonyan & Zisserman, 2014 in Secs. 3.3 and C.2); inconsistent setup counts (37 vs. 34 setups; 7 vs. 9 attacks between Sec. 4.1 and Discussion E); the code URL in the abstract is cut off ('available at:').

The method itself is essentially a single standard data augmentation with one hyper-parameter; the contribution rests on the empirical observation and the feature-space analysis. The latter is only qualitative (PCA scatter plots and convex hulls in Figs. 3, 4, C.4, C.5) — no quantitative measure of feature discrepancy is correlated with attack accuracy, so the causal story for Property P1 remains suggestive rather than rigorously established.

Key headline claims are somewhat stronger than the evidence: 'for the first time, we achieve significant degrade in attack accuracy without decrease in utility' holds only in specific high-resolution configurations (and partly because RE can improve natural accuracy as an augmentation); in the standard low-resolution 64x64 setups, MIDRE's natural accuracy (79.85) is on par with BiDO and below NoDef (86.90), so the 'no utility cost' framing does not generalize.

Some baseline comparisons are incomplete: e.g., BiDO comparisons are limited to T=VGG16 because 'BiDO only releases their implementation and pretrained model in the setup of T = VGG16' (Table B.8), and comparisons to NLS in the main text (Table 3) rely partly on numbers taken from the NLS paper rather than re-run.

The user study results (Tables B.11, B.12) are weaker than the narrative suggests: against TL-DMI, 509 vs. 537 votes is nearly a tie, and the vote-count presentation does not control for rater disagreement across the three raters per pair.

Writing contains numerous grammatical issues throughout ('degrade' as a noun, 'archiving' for 'achieving', 'trade-of', 'acuracy', 'implies' for 'in order to', etc.), which, while individually minor, collectively suggest insufficient polish for a camera-ready-quality submission.
